text: An array holds only zeros, ones and twos — red, white and blue. Sort it in place, so all the zeros come first, then the ones, then the twos. Follow-up: one pass, constant extra space, no library sort.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Exactly three distinct values, and I mutate the input directly? A two-pass counting sort would be trivial — count each value, then overwrite — but the follow-up wants a single pass in place.
Right — see if you can do it in one pass.
That's the Dutch National Flag problem — a three-way partition with three pointers, done in a single sweep.

Let me set up the invariant. This problem reminds me of three-way partitioning, the same step quicksort uses to group keys equal to the pivot. Three pointers: l is the boundary of the zero region, i is the scanner, and r is the boundary of the two region. I maintain four zones: before l, all zeros; from l up to i, all ones; from i through r, unexamined; and after r, all twos. As i scans, I route each value to its zone.

Here's the plan. One: start l and i at zero, and r at the last index, and loop while i is at most r. Two: on a zero, swap it to l, and move both l and i forward. Three: on a two, swap it to r and pull r back, but leave i where it is; on a one, just move i. The crux is the asymmetry. On a zero, I advance i after the swap, because l sits in the already-scanned ones zone, so whatever comes back is a one, already handled. On a two, I do not advance i — the element swapped in from r comes from the unexamined zone, so I must re-check it next iteration. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Let me write it. It's one while loop with three branches: a zero swaps left and advances both l and i; a two swaps right and only pulls r back; a one just advances i. The line that's easy to get wrong is the two branch — writing i plus plus there out of habit would skip the swapped-in value, and if that's a zero it stays stuck in the middle. One detail worth flagging — l is never past i, so the zero swap is safe even when i equals l; it just swaps the element with itself.

Let's dry-run two, zero, two, one, one, zero — expected zero, zero, one, one, two, two. The row that matters is the first one: i sees a two, swaps it with the zero at the end, and r drops to four, but i stays. So the zero swapped in from the right is re-examined on the next iteration — that's why it reaches the left. The rest is routine, and the loop ends when i passes r, with the array sorted. That matches. Corner cases: an empty array, where the loop skips; a single element; and all the same value — they all work.

Time is linear — each step advances i or pulls back r, so the gap from i to r shrinks every iteration: at most n steps, one pass. Space is constant — three pointers, in place. One more thing — this is exactly a three-way quicksort partition with the pivot equal to one, which is the standard trick for arrays with many duplicate keys. For k distinct values instead of three, I'd switch to a two-pass counting sort.
Nicely done. Three things stood out: recognizing the Dutch National Flag, the invariant that justifies advancing i on a zero but not on a two, and connecting it to three-way quicksort. Good work.
